However, 14 other people remained in custody in the African nation, some facing serious charges that could carry prison sentences of up to 20 years.

The journalists were among seven Europeans released Sunday by a Chadian judge, including a Spanish flight crew whom Sarkozy dropped off during a brief stop in Madrid on his return from Chad. All had been arrested last week after workers from Zoe’s Ark — a French-based charity — were accused of attempting to fly 103 children out of Chad as part of a kidnapping and adoption operation.

Some of the children may never be returned to their families because determining their backgrounds could prove too difficult, Red Cross spokeswoman Inah Kaloga told CNN on Friday. Those still under arrest in Chad include six members of the French charity, four Chadians, and four remaining members of the flight crew. Some face charges of kidnapping and fraud.

Zoe’s Ark leader Eric Breteau testified Saturday before a court in the Chadian capital that the three journalists and the flight crew — seven Spaniards and one Belgian — were not involved in the alleged plot, court witnesses told CNN. At least some members of the flight crew are scheduled to testify before a judge on Monday. The three journalists had initially been charged with complicity in the alleged kidnapping attempt. It remains unclear whether the charges against them have been dropped.

At a joint news conference Sunday with Spanish Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero at Madrid’s Torrejón Air Force Base, Sarkozy expressed satisfaction that some of those detained had been released. At the same time, however, he told reporters, “We should respect the sovereignty of Chad.” Zapatero thanked Sarkozy for returning the four Spanish flight crew members to their home country and expressed gratitude to Chadian President Idriss Deby for allowing them to leave.

Following his emergency talks in Chad, Sarkozy emphasized that the scandal would not affect the strong relations between the two countries, nor would it affect the planned deployment of a European force to protect refugees from Sudan’s Darfur region who had fled to Chad and the neighboring Central African Republic. Sarkozy also said he hoped the six remaining French nationals — all members of Zoe’s Ark — would stand trial in France.

The charity says the children were orphans from the Darfur region, where the United Nations estimates that 200,000 people have been killed in four years of conflict, and that it was taking them to host families in France. But after preliminary interviews with the children, aid agencies said Thursday that most of them appeared likely not to be orphans and not to be from Sudan, but rather from villages on the Chadian side of the border with Sudan.

The children are staying in an orphanage in Abeche while aid agencies and government officials attempt to determine where they came from — a challenge complicated by the number of children, their young ages, and the volatile situation in the region.

A father of three of the allegedly kidnapped children told a French newspaper that he had placed his children in the charity’s care after being told they would be educated at a school under construction in a nearby town. The Chadian man, who gave his name as Arbab, told *Le Parisien* on Sunday that workers from Zoe’s Ark had visited his village three times.

“They never said they would take away our children,” he told the newspaper.

CNN’s Nic Robertson and Al Goodman contributed to this report.

**French Journalists Charged in Chad Over Alleged Child Kidnap Plot**

*N’DJAMENA, Chad — October 2007*

Chadian authorities have charged a group of French nationals, including journalists, in connection with an alleged plot to fly more than 100 children out of Chad for adoption in Europe, in a case that has triggered diplomatic alarm in Paris and emergency talks led by French President Nicolas Sarkozy.

The arrests followed an attempt by the French aid group *L’Arche de Zoé* — Zoe’s Ark — to remove 103 children from eastern Chad, a region bordering Sudan’s war-torn Darfur. The organization said it was trying to rescue orphans from the conflict and place them with host families in France and other European countries. Chadian officials, however, accused the group of attempting to kidnap children under the false claim that they were Darfur orphans.

Prosecutors in Chad said the French detainees could face serious charges, including kidnapping and fraud. Among those held were members of Zoe’s Ark, airline crew, and French journalists who had traveled with the group to document the operation. The journalists have denied involvement in any criminal activity, saying they were present only in a professional capacity.

The case has provoked outrage in Chad, where officials said preliminary inquiries suggested many of the children were not Sudanese refugees and may not have been orphans. Aid workers and international agencies have called for caution, stressing that the children’s identities and family circumstances must be verified before any conclusions are reached.

The International Committee of the Red Cross and other humanitarian organizations were expected to assist in tracing the children’s families and determining whether they came from Chad or across the border in Darfur. Relief officials warned that the chaos surrounding the Darfur conflict and the displacement of civilians in eastern Chad had created conditions in which vulnerable children could be easily misidentified or exploited.

In Paris, the affair rapidly became a political crisis. President Sarkozy opened emergency talks with Chadian President Idriss Déby’s government and pledged that France would cooperate with the investigation while seeking fair treatment for its citizens. French officials also moved to distance the government from Zoe’s Ark, saying the operation had not been authorized by Paris and did not conform to international adoption rules.

“This is a grave matter,” a French government source said. “The priority is to establish the truth, protect the children, and ensure that due process is respected.”

Zoe’s Ark had reportedly told European families that it was arranging emergency care for children orphaned by violence in Darfur. But Chadian authorities said the group lacked proper authorization to remove the children and had misrepresented their origins. Witnesses said the children were found bandaged and prepared for evacuation aboard a chartered aircraft when the operation was halted.

The scandal has drawn attention to the complex humanitarian landscape around Darfur, where violence has spilled into eastern Chad and created large refugee camps. International agencies have long warned that child protection in the region is fragile, but they also emphasize that emergency evacuation and international adoption must follow strict legal safeguards.

The arrests have strained relations between France and Chad, a former French colony where Paris maintains significant diplomatic and military ties. Sarkozy’s intervention underscored the sensitivity of the case, with French officials under pressure both to defend detained citizens and to avoid appearing to interfere in Chad’s judicial process.

Chadian officials insisted the case would proceed under Chadian law.

“No one has the right to take children from Chad under false pretenses,” one official said. “If crimes were committed, those responsible must answer for them.”

The fate of the detained journalists remained unclear, though press freedom advocates urged Chadian authorities to distinguish between those who organized the alleged operation and those who were reporting on it. Meanwhile, humanitarian workers began the painstaking process of interviewing the children and tracing their families, a task expected to take weeks.

The case has become one of the most controversial intersections of humanitarian activism, journalism, adoption, and international law in the shadow of the Darfur crisis.

The case erupted after members of Zoe’s Ark, a French aid group, were arrested in eastern Chad while trying to transport 103 children to Europe. The organization said it was conducting a humanitarian operation to rescue orphans from Sudan’s war-torn Darfur region. But Chadian officials accused the group of attempting to illegally remove children from the country, and international agencies later raised doubts about the charity’s claims.

Among those freed were French journalists who had been covering the operation and Spanish flight crew members whose aircraft had been intended to carry the children out of Chad. Their release eased diplomatic tensions with France and Spain, though the central legal case against Zoe’s Ark workers remained unresolved.

Humanitarian officials said the children’s backgrounds were still being investigated. While Zoe’s Ark described them as Darfur orphans in need of evacuation, aid workers from organizations including the United Nations and the Red Cross indicated that many of the children appeared to be Chadian, not Sudanese, and that some may have at least one living parent or relatives.

The uncertainty has intensified criticism of the group’s methods. Chadian authorities have portrayed the attempted airlift as a serious violation of national sovereignty and child-protection laws. The case has also raised broader concerns about emergency humanitarian action, international adoption networks, and the vulnerability of children in conflict zones.

French President Nicolas Sarkozy welcomed the release of the journalists and flight crew but stressed that the remaining detainees would still have to face Chadian justice. Madrid had maintained that the crew members were not responsible for the charity’s alleged actions and had been caught up in the affair while performing their aviation duties.

The Zoe’s Ark controversy has strained relations between Chad and European governments at a time when the region was already under intense international scrutiny because of the conflict in neighboring Sudan and the displacement of refugees across the border.
